evidence: Hor. Epod. 11.10: petītus īmō spīritus, a sigh (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Breathing and the breath drawn: to breathe is spīritum dūcere (also “to be alive”, Cic. Fam. 10.1.1), the last breath spīritus extrēmus. Its other senses are a breeze, pride or spirit, and in Christian Latin the Holy Spirit.

terms.gloss: the breath, the air breathed in and out
evidence: Ter. Ph. 868: animam compressī, I held my breath (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Lewis & Short: anima is the air breathed, spīritus the breathing. So animam recipere, to get one’s breath back, animam continēre, to hold it (see hold one’s breath). Its other sense is the life or soul.

terms.gloss: breath breathed out, its smell; steam
terms.comment: Bad breath is, in Pliny, animae gravitās or ōris graveolentia (M-O s.v. bad breath).

evidence: Plaut. As. 326–327: nōn vidēs mē ex cursūrā anhēlitum etiam dūcere?

phrases.latin: Quid festīnās, mī Geta? Animam recipe.
phrases.english: What’s the hurry, Geta? Catch your breath.

phrases.latin: in pulmōnibus autem inest rāritās quaedam et adsimilis spongiīs mollitūdō ad hauriendum spīritum aptissima
phrases.english: the lungs have a certain looseness, a softness like a sponge’s, made for drawing in breath

phrases.latin: leō cum jacēret spīritum extrēmum trahēns
phrases.english: when the lion lay drawing his last breath
